lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. In just over 1 month's time, the American nation is going to be going to the polls and electing a new president. To say that America is a nation divided would at the least be an accurate statement. Politics have been— become more polarized than ever, and often general debate and discussion is readily labeled as uncompassionate, homophobic, racist, and even hate speech at seemingly a moment's blush. Over the last couple of years, I have heard many commentators and experts talk about the different causes for the decline in the population's ability, both in America and other Western countries, to have healthy discussion and debate on topics that may not even be contentious. And how these discussions devolve into an impasse that ends with a statement such as, to agree to disagree, before either party even genuinely comes to the table to value the other individual's outlook. Some of these experts and commentators have blamed social media and the disconnect and dehumanization of debate through a screen. Other experts lean in on social factors such as a lack of a nuclear family, poverty, and mental health. Thank you. While these can all be looked at as contributing factors, I have found in both dealing with my younger individuals at work, as well as looking at friend circles and peers of my younger children, another causation to the descent of common courteous debate needs to be looked at and hatched out. Something that has always existed in human nature but has become a banner for like minds to rally behind in my— in recent times is a term coined groupthink. I've heard this term used before but never really got down to the core of the word and its technical definition. Groupthink is defined as the practice of thinking or making decisions as a group in a way that discourages creativity or individual responsibility. By this definition, groupthink not only is a discouraging activity to be engaging in, but borderline evil. I, for one, as a parent, would be appalled if my children were being fully immersed in an environment where groupthink was not only encouraged but accepted and mandatory. An environment where an individual's responsibility is no longer encouraged and people are not encouraged to explore their creativity can easily become a slippery slope that can bring down a society. And yet, if you look at major corporations, educational institutions, and government organizations, groupthink is becoming more and more prevalent in our society. Human resource departments are currently falling over themselves across Western society to outdo the To outdo each other, pardon me, by being the grand champion company of diversity, equity, and inclusion, also known by its acronym DEI. Corporations fight to see who can be the most diverse and equitable regardless of an individual's abilities, creativity, or experience. It's not a giant leap to conclude that by hiring under DEI principles, you are working towards a key point in the definition of groupthink. Hmm. Removing an individual's responsibility. If you turn your eye to the government, they do not even try to hide their groupthink. If there is ever a— if ever there is a debate or discussion around legislation on abortion, for example, you should quickly run to YouTube and watch the newest clips of MPs calling each other's names, using unparliamentary language and childish behavior, where grown adults throw their temper tantrums and resort to using insults and name-calling, even from the top parliamentary parliamentarians, we see groupthink on display without any hesitation and almost in a religious fanaticism. Groupthink is also something that we have seen have a glaring light shine on in recent— recently across post-secondary campuses with regards to the Palestinian and Israel conflict. Campuses across North America had been occupied by pro-Palestinian protesters that refused to answer questions, would not open any dialogue with anyone that did not participate as a protester, and and refused to follow law enforcement direction until put under duress or legal force. These— there was no open debate or discussion about what solutions could be worked on, what atrocities were occurring, or what common ground could be found between different groups, but rather the groupthink led to a mob mentality that in some instances led to violence against other students, security, and law enforcement. When individuals engage in groupthink without any consideration of the personal responsibility for what they say, They are doing themselves a disservice in cheapening the words they speak, the values they believe in, and the intelligence that they have. Now, don't get me wrong, it's great to submerge yourself in a friend's group of like minds and principles. I could not think of a more peaceful family gathering than one where everyone agreed on religion, politics, and the economy around the dinner table. However, we as a society as a whole cannot and should not ever find ourselves engaging in groupthink to the point where we stifle someone's opinion, outlook, or ability simply because that is a belief that people you surround yourself have. We are individuals, and everyone we encounter is also an individual. It's time we as society start looking at people as the individuals they are and not look at them for the circles they frequent. It's easy to say, but to break free of your own groupthink is a lifelong journey for many. So thank you, Mr. Mayor. And if you or anyone else disagrees with what I said today, I hope it's because of the specific words I spoke and not because someone in your group told you what to think.
